summary: observation of a luminous disk changing shape and color.
description: On December 23rd and 24th, 1981, between 6:30 PM and 7:00 PM, several people observed a peculiar luminous phenomenon in the cloudy sky. Circular in shape, this phenomenon changed color several times, shifting from white to orange. Initially stationary, this phenomenon appeared to have moved, which would explain why it was seen growing and shrinking at times. Pilots and air traffic controllers also noticed this glow on December 24th. Despite a thorough investigation by the gendarmerie with various services and verification using astronomy software, we lack sufficient information to confirm that the witnesses observed Venus, which was particularly visible that evening.

summary: Observation of a luminous yellow-orange phenomenon twinkling in the night sky towards the SE: observation of Sirius.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as A, B, C, or D, which are now being re-examined to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This observation, previously classified as D and named LANN-BIHOUE (56) 1981, is one of a group of cases recently re-examined. On December 21, 1981, at approximately 10:10 PM, a family observed a round, orange, luminous object in the southeast sky for 10 minutes. The witness reports that the object moved at very high speed with straight-line movements and abrupt changes of direction at sharp angles. This point was surrounded by flashes of light of the same color that appeared and disappeared alternately for about ten minutes. This phenomenon then disappeared to the south, and a second glow to the east, but at a lower altitude, could be seen for a few seconds before disappearing completely. Only one witness account was recorded. Regarding the main phenomenon (observed over 10 minutes), the witnesses probably observed the star Sirius, which happened to be low on the southeastern horizon at the time of the observation, and in the direction of the observation (see the investigation report). Favorable observing conditions with a clear sky, but with some passing low clouds, could have caused this confusion, as the star twinkled strongly and could have been obscured after about ten minutes by the passage of a bank of low clouds. The witness's description of the presence of flashes of light is consistent with the hypothesis, because at this elevation the celestial body twinkles randomly, its light rays passing through a thicker atmospheric layer more prone to atmospheric turbulence. The description of movements in both elevation and azimuth, at a very high speed, is also consistent with and reinforces the hypothesis. Indeed, the fact that the witness felt the need to mention that these movements had a tendency to shift southward indicates that the overall angular movement of the UFO over 10 minutes (observation time) remained small. We can conclude that this is the natural physiological phenomenon of micro-ocular mobility (emicro-nystagmus), little known to the general public, which occurs when one stares at objects, particularly at night. This translates into the false impression that bright point objects are affected by small, aberrant movements, such as zigzags. Two elements prevent us from firmly confirming this hypothesis: - the witness does not indicate the UFO's altitude in the sky, although we can deduce from their comparison to a landing aircraft that it was a low altitude, consistent with that of Sirius; - the presence of some clouds. A cloud may have obstructed Sirius, whereas, in the definite absence of clouds, at least in that direction, the fact that the witness did not notice Sirius in the vicinity of the UFO would constitute further proof that the UFO and Sirius are being confused. Nevertheless, in light of all the other converging elements, the Sirius hypothesis has a probability well above 50% and must be accepted. The second phenomenon is much more fleeting, and unlike the first, we have very little evidence to establish and test any hypothesis. The consistency of the testimony is average, with only one witness account despite the presence of several, and the data for the first observation is fragmentary and imprecise, while the data for the second is very insufficient. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies the first phenomenon as category B: Sirius observation. The testimony regarding the second phenomenon is unusable.

summary: Long observations of the slow and silent movement of about a hundred luminous objects in the sky: probable observations of festive balloons (balloons).
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as A, B, C, or D, which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even an explicit change in classification within an investigation report. This observation, previously classified as D and named NICE (06) 1981, is part of a group of cases recently re-examined. On Saturday, December 19, 1981, between 10:30 and 10:50 AM, several witnesses observed between 50 and 100 flying objects very high in the sky. These objects were mostly round, white, and shiny, moving southwest in a single formation with unequal distances between each object. They moved slowly and made no noise. The last three objects had a different shape, like a tube. These changed color, alternating between white and orange. These objects disappeared, hidden by the landscape and clouds. Two witnesses filed reports with the police. The witnesses' description of the UFO(s) strongly resembled a group balloon release (see the investigation notes). It is worth noting that the sighting occurred on a Saturday morning, the last day of school before the 1981 Christmas holidays. With Christmas just a week away, the sighting could thus be explained by a mass balloon release with letters written by students. The trajectory described as northeast to southwest appears reliable, as witnesses indicated the same direction and saw the UFOs pass close to their vertical (which helps in estimating the direction of movement). This direction is not exactly that of the wind, which is from north to south. However, it should be noted: - that the wind was measured at sea level, while the potential balloons were moving 6 km above sea level and at an altitude of over 100 m (given their small size), and perhaps even higher, as they were likely launched from the hills above Nice; - that the area is urban and near mountains (factors that contribute to local variations). These are all elements that could explain why the wind at the UFOs had a direction 40 degrees different from that measured at the Nice weather station. Furthermore, the wind measured from noon onwards was from east to west and could therefore have started to shift slightly earlier at the altitude of the UFOs. Furthermore, the slow speed and duration of the UFO's journey are consistent with a light wind measured at around 7 km/h. The appearance of the colors and glare of the UFOs varies depending on the witnesses. T2 observes different colors between UFOs with round shapes and different colors (yellow-green-red-blue); T1 observes a bright white color giving a reflection resembling that of light on an aluminum plate. These two descriptions are compatible with balloons of seemingly different colors strongly reflecting the sun (the sun-balloon-witness geometry is conducive to reflection). T1 distinguishes different UFOs (at the end of formation). The shape is no longer round but that of tubes, and the color of each alternates between orange and white. This can be explained by the introduction into this swarm, which was largely composed of round balloons, of a few more complex, cylindrical balloons with two faces and different colors. It should be noted that T2 did not distinguish any UFOs from the others, apart from the fact that some of them lit up and others went out. On this last point, both testimonies can be explained by the asymmetrical shape of (some) balloons, which facilitated spinning and therefore variations in reflection or color depending on the actual balloons or the particularities and precision of the witnesses' perceptions. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies the case as B: probable observation of festive balloons (flash balloons).

summary: Observation of a bright point at very high altitude.
description: On December 16, 1981, an hour after sunset, several witnesses observed a bright point surrounded by a bluish ring. This point sometimes appeared with a colored trail. Its movements formed zigzags. No other information could be gathered about this phenomenon.

summary: Observation of a luminous phenomenon.
description: On December 6, 1981, at approximately 8:35 PM, witnesses observed a peculiar luminous phenomenon in the sky. All noticed a series of luminous circular shapes moving at irregular speeds within a limited area. No sound was heard, and the phenomenon remained visible for about an hour before disappearing over the horizon. We lack sufficient data to propose any hypothesis regarding the origin of this phenomenon.

summary: An unusual object was observed at an airfield. The CRNA (Regional Air Navigation Center) reported the acquisition of a spot visible on radar at the time the phenomenon was observed.
description: On November 22, 1981, between 7:40 and 8:00 AM, several people were on the road surrounding the airfield. It was not yet fully dawn, but visibility was good. Suddenly, they spotted a reddish-orange sphere hovering motionless above the field just before the airfield. This sphere, about the size of a soccer ball, disappeared abruptly and appeared to have fallen into the field; at no point did the witnesses hear any unusual noise. On duty that morning, two gendarmes also observed, around 8:00 AM, a luminous orange sphere moving along the runway as if preparing to land, just as a plane on the same runway was about to take off. As the sphere descended, it became larger. The firefighter immediately alerted the control tower, but the object vanished instantly. No noise was heard by witnesses, and no traces were found in the field or on the runway. Nevertheless, the CRNA reported a spot visible on radar between 7:50 and 8:04 AM. This phenomenon remains unexplained.

summary: Sirius observation
description: On November 28, 1981, at 12:45 a.m., two gendarmes on duty observed an extremely bright light in the sky. It was stationary and appeared to be flashing. Using binoculars, they could distinguish flashes of light of various colors around its perimeter. These flashes flickered on and off randomly. The gendarmes, who had a star chart, located the light to the left of the constellation Orion. This observation lasted several hours. After checking with astronomy software, these witnesses determined that they had most likely seen Sirius that night, a star particularly visible in the sky at that time of year.

summary: observation of a luminous phenomenon at the edge of a wood.
description: On November 21, 1981, around 8:00 PM, two people spotted a peculiar luminous phenomenon in the woods opposite their home, which intrigued them. The object, rectangular in shape, was reddish-orange and remained motionless. During the observation, which lasted nearly an hour, the witnesses saw a green halo gradually encircle the rectangle, followed by two very powerful spotlights emitting a yellow light. The object slowly rose into the air at a 45° angle before disappearing into the sky. No sound was heard during the observation. The next day, one of the witnesses went to the site but found no trace of it. The police were notified 25 days later, and no trace of it could be found on the ground or in the surrounding area, nor did any other witnesses come forward to provide further information.

summary: Observation of the probable reentry of an object into the atmosphere
description: On November 20, 1981, around 6:00 PM, several witnesses observed a luminous sphere in the sky followed by a multicolored trail. This sphere moved at very high speed, crossing the sky in a south-north direction. The observation lasted 15 to 30 seconds under a clear sky. One of the witnesses heard a whistling sound. These people likely witnessed an atmospheric reentry.

summary: Long night observation of a very bright phenomenon in a field: very likely observation of one or more agricultural machine(s).
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, classified at the time (A, B, C, or D), which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This case, previously classified as D and named FEIGNIES (59) 06.11.1981, is part of a group of cases recently re-examined. On November 6, 1981, at approximately 7:45 PM, a witness observed a very intense luminous phenomenon behind his house and "near a utility pole" in a field. The observation lasted approximately one hour, and when the light went out, the witness saw a cigar-shaped object in a vertical position surrounded by various colors. Subsequently, these lights went out, revealing an object shaped like a metallic gray rugby ball. For four to five seconds, this object swayed from side to side before returning to its vertical position. The witness then observed an orange corridor in the sky "coming from the location of this craft," as well as white trails. No noise was heard during the observation. The witness reported having already observed luminous phenomena near her home the previous week. The Gendarmerie was not notified of this observation until 10 days later. No other witnesses for this date and observation area were found. The analysis is based on: - the official report of the witness's statements; - aerial photographs and maps from that time and today; - of the private investigation conducted in the days following the observation (Lumières Dans La Nuit (LDLN) magazine, January-February 1984, nos. 235-236), part of which is attached to the official report. No element of this private investigation is used to support the conclusion, which rests solely on the other elements. On the other hand, the elements of this investigation, which would appear to contradict the hypothesis adopted, are used to distinguish the elements strictly attributable to the witness from the interpretations or conclusions implicitly or explicitly deduced from the investigation. We conclude that the witness, newly arrived (two months) and probably unfamiliar with the area and local agricultural practices, most likely observed one or more agricultural machines carrying out nighttime work in the adjacent fields, specifically collecting piles of beets harvested in the preceding days and stacked along a farm track easily accessible from the road to the east (see the investigation report). This conclusion is based on the following points: - similar observations having taken place in the preceding days; - nighttime work related to beet harvesting probably already existed in 1981, with spotlights equipping the dedicated machines; - we are in the middle of the beet harvesting season, and beet fields are located not far from the witness's house, in the direction of observation; - The harvesting work, probably already underway on all or part of nearby plots in the preceding days, was completed shortly (10 days) after the observation, according to the private investigation; - the PAN (Population Access Point) appeared to be on the ground, according to the witness; - strong lights were present, comparable to the headlights of agricultural machinery; - the measurements and calculations of distances and dimensions, although necessarily imprecise due to poor observation conditions, are consistent with the observation of such machinery. The distance could be roughly between approximately 250 and 500 m, with the farm track located approximately 400/450 m from the witness, along the observation line; - the observation period was long, consistent with the time required for harvesting the beets; - The shape of the UFO was imprecise and changing, caused by a perceptual illusion of shape at night; - The movements of the agricultural harvesting machine, going back and forth around the piles of beets, are consistent with the witness's description of horizontal movement with back-and-forth motions; - The orange corridor observed by the witness once the machine had moved is reminiscent of what can be observed when a spotlight is pointed towards the sky under favorable atmospheric conditions (mist, fog, humidity). It could be one of the work lights, left on for a time (duration not specified by the witness) unnecessarily (which could explain being pointed towards the sky). This is a plausible hypothesis that no evidence can confirm or refute. - These agricultural machines are noisy, but the observation conditions (behind a window, television on, and observation distance) may explain why the witness did not perceive any noise. Two aspects of the observation (derived exclusively from the private investigation) appear to fit less well with the hypothesis: - the observation of thin, multicolored beams around the UFO. The hypothesis of a light diffraction phenomenon caused by condensation on the French window, generated by the witness, was considered; however, it can occur under certain conditions (significant temperature difference, high humidity, and a short distance between the witness and the window), only the last of which could not be confirmed due to a lack of precision regarding the distance; - the observation of the UFO, in a specific phase, in front of the pole. The (brief) mention in the private investigation was not made directly by the witness, and the drawing used to support this information was also not made by the witness. Furthermore, no explanation is given as to what would have concretely led the witness to believe that the UFO was passing in front of the pole. The factual elements needed to evaluate the claim are lacking: no comparative data on the colors of the UFO/background, no data on the brightness of the lights at that moment. The mention of the ground illuminated by the UFO, which was not visible to the witness, is not inconsistent with its position near the pole, nor is it inconsistent with its position further away, near the farm track, therefore behind the pole. Furthermore, doubts exist regarding the nature of the profiling of the post visible to the witness: it could be due to the contrast with the background of the moonlit landscape or to the brightness of the UFO. The report is mediocre, with a rather in-depth description of the UFO and the various observation phases. However, it is sufficient to draw a conclusion, given the high probability of the chosen hypothesis (low resulting strangeness). Consequently, GEIPAN classifies it as A: highly probable observation of one or more agricultural vehicles harvesting beets on a farm track located along the observation line.

summary: Observation of a flying object at very high altitude.
description: On November 4, 1981, roofers observed a round, slowly moving flying object at a high altitude around 10:00 AM. Visible for about ten minutes, witnesses saw several colors or lights that appeared to flash or appear as the object rotated. The sky was clear, providing good visibility. The object then disappeared into the landscape. No further information was gathered about this phenomenon, which remains unexplained due to a lack of data.

summary: Observation of the flight of an advertising balloon.
description: On November 1, 1981, around 11:00 AM, several witnesses spotted a flying object moving slowly towards the sea. This gray, cylindrical object was approximately 4 meters long. No noise was heard during its movement. The investigation determined that it was an advertising balloon launched by children from the terrace of the "Le Corbusier" building, about 300 meters from the observation point.

summary: Sighting of a very bright object.
description: On November 1, 1981, several people in a vehicle observed a stationary object about 30 meters above a field, approximately 100 meters away. Driving slowly, the witnesses noted that the craft had a hemispherical shape and a fluorescent color. A spotlight directed towards the ground at the bottom right edge emitted an intermittent white light. A kind of heat emission blurred the object's outline. After dropping someone off at their home and driving past the field again, they discovered the object had disappeared. The investigation failed to uncover any traces or other witnesses to this phenomenon, for which we lack sufficient data.

summary: Observations of a luminous phenomenon resembling a neon tube and stationary in the direction of the rising sun: lack of information.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as A, B, C, or D, which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This observation, previously classified as D and named SAINT-PIERRE (974) 1981, is part of a group of cases recently re-examined (see the investigation report). On October 22, 1981, at 8:30 a.m., a driver and his passenger were intrigued by a white, stationary, low-altitude light phenomenon that they could not explain. The UFO, shaped like a line with a circle underneath (T1) or a rectangle (T2), was located in the direction of the rising sun. The driver stopped his vehicle. He then considered taking out the theodolite located at the rear of the vehicle to observe the UFO more closely, but the two witnesses were essentially paralyzed in the car. According to the two witnesses, the observation of this "neon tube" lasted approximately 5 minutes before the UFO gradually disappeared, according to T1, or almost instantaneously, according to T2. Despite an article appearing in the local press, no other witness statements were collected. The witnesses were able to observe an aircraft contrail under favorable atmospheric conditions, with the sun quite low behind the aircraft and illuminating the contrail. This trail is of a particular type with ragged edges, here with a single ragged edge: - the process of aircraft trail formation and persistence involves several atmospheric factors (including pressure and humidity) that can vary along an aircraft's trajectory, even without changing altitude; - if the process allows for formation and high persistence throughout the flight, the trail will be long and continuous behind the aircraft, subject only to the effect of wind, which can widen, disperse, or twist it; - if the process allows for formation but with low persistence throughout the flight, the trail will be short and give the impression of following the aircraft; - if the formation and persistence processes vary along the trajectory, the trail may be ragged or even limited to a single, fixed, persistent end, as is probably the case here. The website Contrail Science provides examples with photographs. The round, less luminous shape observed beneath the streak by T1 is, in the absence of any consistent angular indication of dispersion and local broadening of the trail. It is also unclear whether the round shape is adjacent to or distant from the streak. It could also be a nebula located away from the streak, whose particularly round shape leads T1 to associate it with the streak's strangeness, whereas he would have noticed nothing without the initial strangeness. This shape is perceived by T1 as more difficult to distinguish than the streak; it is possible that T2 (who did not see it) does not have the same visual capacity or attentional capacity as T1, or did not associate a nebula with the initial strangeness. The disappearance of the trail, as perceived by T2, appears too rapid. However, the hypothesis of reduced visual acuity or attention on the part of T2 could also explain why he only saw the beginning of the decrease in light intensity, while T1 was able to follow the phenomenon as it gradually faded. The consistency is mediocre in both information and reliability: - the description lacks precision, particularly in terms of angular position in the sky, angular size, and the respective positions of the two shapes seen by T1. - there are two (non-independent) witnesses whose accounts corroborate each other on some points and are discordant on others. These discrepancies in accounts have not led to any requests for clarification to better quantify the degree of discordance beyond the words themselves. The lack of information and certain discrepancies lead to the development of complementary hypotheses to explain the observation by a trail. In fact, the aircraft-trail hypothesis loses probability but remains plausible. Ultimately, the evidence proves too weak to validate such an explanation. These two factors—the existence of a plausible hypothesis but a lack of sufficient evidence to support it—prevent the object from remaining in the unexplained UAP category. Consequently, GEIPAN concludes: lack of reliable information.

summary: Observations of the movement of a cylindrical object, tin-white or aluminum in color, reflecting the sun's rays: probable mistaking for an airplane.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as A, B, C, or D, which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This observation, previously classified as D, is one of a group of cases recently re-examined. On October 14, 1981, between 2:30 and 2:45 PM, two witnesses observed a cylindrical object moving silently across the sky for one minute. No wings or fins were observed. Of moderate strangeness and good consistency (two dependent witnesses), this case appears to be a probable case of mistaken identity involving an aircraft (see the investigation report). Several details in the testimonies strongly suggest the hypothesis of mistaken identity, notably the appearance of a wingless fuselage, a feature now well-known to GEIPAN (the French UFO research group): the geometry of the witness, aircraft, and sun means that the sun's rays are reflected only onto the fuselage and not onto the wings (one obscured, the other with a reflection surface limited to the edge). An approach corridor for Marseille airport passes just north of the observation site, with an orientation perfectly consistent with the UFO's trajectory. The strangeness of the case lies primarily in the fact that the witnesses did not see a wing or fin on the UFO, and that it was believed to be close to the witnesses. However, the witnesses, in another classic error when an object or phenomenon is not recognized, were unable to correctly estimate the actual distance separating them from the UAP. The hypothesis of a misidentification with a weather balloon can also be put forward based on the testimonies, but it turns out that the results of a local radiosonde show that the winds were blowing against the direction of the UAP's movement. The case is class B, probable misidentification with an aircraft.

summary: Observation of a concrete block crossing the road.
description: On October 5, 1981, between 9:00 and 10:00 AM, a woman and her passenger were driving on a main road. They suddenly saw a black object resembling a pointed concrete block slowly crossing the road from left to right directly in front of their car. The sighting lasted two seconds before the object disappeared. No further information has been gathered about this phenomenon, for which we lack data.

summary: Observations of the presence of lights on the ground in a field in the middle of the night: unusable as it exceeds the sole competence of GEIPAN.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as A, B, C, or D, which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This case, previously classified as D and named SAINT-HILAIRE (91) 04.10.1981, is part of a group of cases recently re-examined. This concerns the sighting of a UFO (Unidentified Floating Object) by a couple of motorists at the crossroads known as "Pierrot's Cabin" in the commune of Saint-Hilaire (91) during the night of October 3-4, 1981, at approximately 2:30 a.m. The witnesses were surprised to see flashes on the ground, followed by three red lights, also at ground level, which appeared to be moving towards them. Frightened, they quickly left the scene. No noise was heard. The Gendarmerie was notified on October 9 and went to the location but found no trace of the UFO. Only one witness statement was recorded by the gendarmerie on November 3, 1981. Preliminary note concerning a case where the witness statements and evidence relate to a phenomenon explicitly described or observed on the ground: - in the absence of evidence that the ground phenomenon could only have originated and/or departed by air, the search for an explanation exceeds the sole competence of GEIPAN, and a GEIPAN conclusion can only be formulated if proof or near-proof is established; otherwise, GEIPAN must conclude C: Unusable because it exceeds the sole competence of GEIPAN. - conversely, the absence of witness statements or evidence of phases of the phenomenon above ground may lead GEIPAN to be unable to conclude due to a lack of reliable information (standard GEIPAN classification C). We are dealing here with the first scenario, since nothing allows us to rule out that this phenomenon originated or departed from the ground, as the absence of traces in the ground proves nothing either way. The case is therefore classified as Class C: Unusable because it exceeds the sole expertise of GEIPAN. Nevertheless, GEIPAN provides, without any conclusion other than the preceding one, an analysis according to its methods of certain aspects of the case (see the investigation report). The lights, clearly observed to originate from the ground, are difficult to explain in terms of vehicles: - the successive sighting of white and red lights, as well as the evolution of the light configuration, could correspond to changes in viewing angles or changes in the orientation of a vehicle; - an agricultural machine in operation could thus have a particular lighting pattern with a single headlight at the front (perceived as successive flashes due to variations in its pointing) and three red lights at the rear. But agricultural or other activities undertaken by the owner or operator are unlikely at 2:30 a.m. on a Sunday. However, the owner, who had been identified, was not questioned; - the possibility of trespassing on the property cannot be ruled out either, as the context of returning from a Saturday night party could encourage inappropriate actions or accidents. The unusual lighting could only be explained by vehicles (several motorcycles?) or specific vehicle configurations; - no tracks were visible in the field, which does not, however, exclude the presence of a vehicle at the time of the incident, particularly if the ground was dry; The perception that witnesses had at the end of the observation of lights approaching them could correspond to the reality of the movement or to a phenomenon known to GEIPAN: the witnesses interpret the increase in intensity of a light (which could be caused here by a better alignment of the lights in the direction of the witnesses) as an advance of these lights towards them. The hypothesis raised is challenged by the question of its plausibility at the time and place, without being able to be ruled out. On the other hand, the case is weak in terms of information and reliability: the witnesses did not give a spontaneous statement. It was rumor that led to the intervention of a GEIPAN correspondent and then to the questioning by the gendarmes. Under these conditions, a witness may find their testimony constrained by previous, hastily given descriptions and by the interpretation (and potentially heightened sense of strangeness) that may have been made and disseminated; - there is only one testimony. The identical description (to the point that the police only considered one testimony) may indicate strong collusion and influence between witnesses prior to being summoned by the police; - there is no description of the UFO's disappearance, and no record of angular dimensions; - the owner of the land where the phenomenon is located was not questioned.

summary: Observation of a strange bright spot in a photograph.
description: Sometime between 11 PM and 1 AM in October 1981, a person was finishing a roll of film, taking the last shots from their parents' apartment. They were photographing the city lights. After the slides were developed by a private lab, they noticed a peculiar point of light on one of them. Having a 13x18 print made, they then saw an object foreign to the natural surroundings and resembling a flying saucer. They decided to file a report with the police and left a sketch of the photograph. No further information was gathered about this sighting.

summary: Recent testimony (2013) of an old observation (1981). Observation of the silent movements of several red-orange lights outlining a dark mass; rapid disappearance: lack of information (uncertain date and no corroboration).
description: Recent testimony (September 2013) of an old sighting (uncertain date, day and month: October/November). The witness recounts an observation made probably in October 1981 at approximately 11:00 PM and lasting 2 to 3 minutes (the date of Saturday, October 17th is given arbitrarily). The witness, bored by a TV series, looked out the patio door and was surprised to see 5 to 6 red-orange dots slowly passing in a straight line around the edge of a dark object. After 1 to 2 minutes, the UFO reversed direction and then ascended before disappearing suddenly into the clear sky. The witness reports a change of color (white) during the acceleration. No unusual noise was heard during the sighting. Another witness observed the event and reported by email in January 2014 seeing a string of red bulbs positioned in a semicircle to the west. The UFO disappeared and then reappeared, speeding off towards the northwest in the sky. No other eyewitness accounts of the phenomenon have been collected. The possibility of mistaking it for an agricultural or construction vehicle with a peculiar and surprising configuration (a passing vehicle other than the owner's, who was asleep) is not entirely ruled out despite the late hour (11 PM in October or November). This was, in fact, the witness's initial hypothesis. This hypothesis is contradicted by the height of the lights described (4 or 5 meters in the trees), and especially by the UFO's rapid disappearance and significant elevation in the sky. The age of the observation and the uncertainty surrounding the date (October or November 1981) make it impossible to explore this aircraft hypothesis. And lacking any other hypothesis, this observation remains strange. On the other hand, this testimony was given more than 30 years later, and is therefore subject to inaccuracies or memory errors. The second observer (spouse) describes a similar phenomenon but with far fewer details. This observer did not wish to testify (a short email was sent to the investigator). The observers did not leave their house to approach the location, remaining within 30 or 35 meters of where the UFO had appeared. This occurred the following day, indicating that the experience was not very intense, nor even particularly strong or frightening, as the witness reports not having been unduly disturbed, even though aware of witnessing something astonishing. It is therefore an observation that remains strange because it lacks an explanation with a probability greater than 20%. However, this observation also lacks consistency, namely information and reliability (30 years later, no precise date, an observer present who does not wish to testify). Consequently, GEIPAN classifies it as C: lack of reliable information.

summary: Observation of low-altitude glows with rapid movements.
description: On September 22, 1981, starting at 3:30 a.m., several witnesses, including police officers, observed lights of different colors at low altitude. The weather was rainy and stormy, which prevented the witnesses from providing a precise description of these lights or their origin. The white light was quickly identified as coming from a radio relay station. However, the red light, which appeared intermittently, and the constant green light were not clearly identified. These lights moved very quickly and erratically. No noise was heard during the entire observation. Furthermore, the main witness reported feeling a very strong hot wind, about which we have no further information.

summary: observation of a luminous object of elliptical shape.
description: On September 22, 1981, at 6:15 a.m., a witness observed a flying object from his bedroom window, moving along a northwest-southeast trajectory. During the one-minute observation, the witness saw an elliptical object with blurred edges and a dome-like shape at its upper surface. The object emitted a yellow-orange light. No other person in the vicinity witnessed this apparition, about which we lack further information.

summary: Observation of the passage of a stationary object shaped like an airplane
description: On September 19, October 3, and October 27, 1981, witnesses observed a luminous object moving across the sky in the same Franco-Spanish border area between 11:00 PM and 3:00 AM. The object's direction in all three sightings was north-south, and all three witnesses reported it as being red. A thorough investigation by the gendarmerie ruled out confusion with known aircraft or celestial bodies but failed to identify the phenomenon.

summary: observation of rapidly moving objects.
description: On September 5th and 6th, 1981, the Lourdes police brigade took statements from people who had seen luminous objects in the sky. These objects moved at high speed and silently at low altitude. The very short observation times (5 seconds) did not allow for enough information to formulate any hypothesis about the observed phenomena.

summary: observation of a trapezoidal glow on the moon.
description: On September 5th, around 11:00 PM, four people noticed a peculiar luminous phenomenon in a pine grove near their home. Trapezoidal in shape, this intense glow was observed for approximately 10 minutes before abruptly disappearing. No sound was heard. At 11:45 PM, the police arrived on the scene but found no trace of the glow. An investigation the following day revealed a circle of ferns, 20 to 30 cm in diameter, all lying in the same direction. The gendarmerie brigade, stationed at the same location the following evening, determined that the phenomenon was caused by moonlight filtering through the pine trees. It was later established that the marks on the ground were left by forestry equipment.

summary: Observation of 3 luminous white and red flashing balls moving silently together: lack of information.
description: This case, formerly known as PARCQ (62) 1981, was recently re-examined (see the Investigation Notes document). On August 11, 1981, around 1:00 AM, a farmer driving his tractor in a field observed red and white orbs flashing in the sky. Initially stationary, these orbs moved slowly from north to south. Panicked, the witness returned home where he continued to see the lights. The police investigation failed to find any other witnesses or evidence to explain this phenomenon. This case is weak (single witness, brief testimony collected several days after the events, no field investigation), and the description of the observed UFO is imprecise. The witness's sincerity and credibility have never been questioned. The described phenomenon shares some characteristics (duration of observation, shape, color) with the Moon, possibly obscured by clouds. It is noted that the Moon was visible in the sky at the time of the observation, but was not mentioned by the witness. However, the testimony provided lacks the necessary details to formally validate this hypothesis. The phenomenon also exhibits certain aspects of luminous phenomena associated with thunderstorm activity. Fatigue after a long day of work and the panic experienced by the witness may have significantly impaired their perception or recollections. In the current GEIPAN classification, this case of moderate strangeness is classified as UAP C, due to a lack of reliable data and corroborating evidence.

summary: Observation of a luminous halo in a photograph of the night sky.
description: On August 6, 1981, around 1:00 AM, a person was taking photographs of the starry sky from the parking lot at the Col de Joux. The weather was clear, without clouds, but occasional heat lightning flashes appeared in the distance. His camera was mounted on a tripod, and each photo was taken with an exposure time of one minute and thirty seconds. During development, the witness noticed the presence of a luminous phenomenon in his photographs that he hadn't seen when he took the pictures. This object was located in a halo to the left of the star Arcturus. A star chart for that day and time clearly shows Arcturus in the constellation Boötes. However, no other information allowed for the identification of the photographed phenomenon.

summary: Observation of a low-altitude flying object.
description: On August 3, 1981, at approximately 10:55 PM, a witness observed a very slow-moving object close to the ground for about 40 seconds, less than 400 meters away. As it passed, a halo of light illuminated the landscape. The object was rounded at the front and emitted a large, multi-colored flame. It moved along an east-west trajectory with a slight downward tilt. Fearing it might strike the mountain, the witness expected to hear an impact, but nothing occurred. The subsequent investigation yielded no further information to explain the observation.

summary: Observation of a zigzagging object at high altitude.
description: On August 3, 1981, at approximately 10:45 PM, several people observed a zigzagging object at a very high altitude. Its trajectory was east-west, and it was moving at very high speed. The luminous object emitted flashing white and red lights. No noise was heard during the observation, which lasted less than five minutes. No explanation for this phenomenon could be found due to a lack of data.

summary: Observation of a luminous phenomenon of red colour, probably the setting sun.
description: On August 1, 1981, at approximately 8:30 PM, a motorist spotted a red fireball due west, which then split in two. Gradually diminishing and changing to a more orange color, this phenomenon disappeared, merging with the mist. No sound was heard during the observation. Some details suggest a possible observation of the setting sun, as indicated by two of the witnesses.

summary: Observation of a cigar-shaped object, with a change of direction.
description: On July 28, 1981, at approximately 12:30 PM, two people on their terrace saw a black dot appear in the sky. As it grew larger, it resembled a cigar. Observed through binoculars, this object frequently changed direction and appeared to be quite large. Bright in the sunlight, it disappeared as it rose due west. No further information was gathered about this phenomenon, which could be interpreted as a passing airplane, but about which we have absolutely no details.

summary: Observation of 2 points of light changing direction.
description: On July 27, 1981, at approximately 11:30 PM, two witnesses observed two bright points in the sky. They moved parallel to each other, then changed trajectory before returning to their starting point. The observation, which lasted about 10 minutes, allowed for the observation of several back-and-forth movements. The objects suddenly moved rapidly westward and disappeared. No sound was heard during the observation. No other accounts have been collected regarding this phenomenon, about which we lack information.

summary: Observation for a few seconds of a torch-shaped flying object.
description: On July 16, 1981, at approximately 11:45 PM, several witnesses on a boat spotted a flying object, larger than a star, above the island of Port-Cros. This object, described as torch-shaped, was white-green in color. During the observation, which lasted several seconds, the object moved slowly along a horizontal trajectory. No further information was gathered about this phenomenon.

summary: Probable observation of the effects of lightning in a maes field
description: On June 12, 1981, in the late afternoon, a farm worker working on a plot of corn noticed a circular area approximately 20 meters in diameter where the plants appeared diseased. In the center of the area, some plants had disappeared, and further out, the plants were withered as if from intense heat, this effect diminishing with distance from the center of the circle and disappearing at about ten meters. In the center, the soil was cracked, and a depression about 80 cm in diameter had formed, containing five holes 4 to 5 cm in diameter and about 20 cm deep, the whole forming a shape resembling a trapezoid. An indefinable odor persisted in the center of the circle. Soil and vegetation samples were taken for further analysis. These analyses confirmed that the central area had been subjected to intense heat. Indeed, it exhibits a significantly lower humidity level than samples taken further away. The temperature experienced in this area is likely above 100°C. Meteorological data indicates that a severe thunderstorm struck the area on the night of June 8-9, bringing heavy rainfall. The lightning hypothesis is favored as it explains the blast effect that the corn plants in the affected area appear to have experienced, as well as the temperature increase at the center of the zone. Currents induced in the ground by a lightning strike could also explain the observed holes.

summary: Observation of a luminous object above the sea: astronomical observation of the Moon.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as type C, which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even an explicit change in classification within an investigation report. This particular observation was classified as type C in 1981 by GEIPAN. On June 7, 1981, around 11:00 PM, two witnesses observed a luminous object in the direction of the sea. Above this object was a crescent-shaped star that gradually transformed and enlarged. The object itself remained in the same position and disappeared after approximately eight minutes. The described phenomenon shares many characteristics (duration of observation, shape, size, color) with a well-known astronomical object: the Moon at sunset. Furthermore, the Moon was clearly visible in the observed area of the sky, even though the witnesses made no mention of it. In the current GEIPAN classification, this case of a weak anomaly is classified as UAP A, an observation linked to a misidentification of the Moon.

summary: Observations by four witnesses in a car of a stationary oval mass with colored lights at low altitude: probable observation of a forestry vehicle.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, classified at the time (A, B, C, or D), which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This case, previously classified as D and named TERNAY (41) 22.05.1981, is part of a group of cases recently re-examined (the case is also known as MONTOIRE (41) 1980). On May 23, 1981, at approximately 11:40 PM, four members of a family were driving on the CD4 (in the commune of Ternay, Loir-et-Cher). They spotted (with difficulty due to very cloudy weather) a bright, low-altitude object. The driver stopped, intrigued by the UFO, which was now located near a grove of trees. The observation, which lasted about fifteen minutes, allowed the witnesses to see an oval-shaped object with lights of several colors (white and blue-green) and, at times, red-orange lights at its extremities. The object, which seemed to emit beams of light, remained motionless. No sound was heard. The UFO disappeared behind the grove of trees. The driver continued on his way, taking the D116 towards Saint-Martin-des-Bois (Loir-et-Cher) to drop off two family members. Two of the four witnesses then returned to the scene by another vehicle. Route. Upon reaching the grove, a thick fog suddenly enveloped the woods. The witnesses turned back. A final glance towards the grove revealed small reddish-orange lights near the ground. The witnesses left the area to return home. The investigation, which took place the following morning, found no trace on the ground or in the surrounding vegetation. Our analysis (see the investigation report) has shown that the witnesses, placed in unfavorable observation conditions (a very dark night environment), were unable to identify an agricultural vehicle, or more likely a forestry vehicle, working at night in a field or a small wood located approximately 2 km from their position. This observation distance, combined with the impossibility of distinguishing the sky/ground boundary under these unfavorable conditions, led the witnesses to believe that the unidentified phenomenon was in the sky, at a low altitude, whereas we were able to demonstrate that it could The object was actually on the ground, in a sloping area with a higher elevation than the witnesses. We therefore explored two hypotheses: that of an agricultural vehicle working in the fields and that of a forestry vehicle carrying out logging or wood maintenance work at night. Although both hypotheses explain the appearance of the UFO (particularly the bright lights), the second is preferred because it provides a better explanation, especially since a small wooded area was located along the observation line. A comparison of aerial photographs taken in May 1978 and July 1981 shows that the wood was cut between these two dates. There is therefore every reason to believe that logging had already begun on the date of the observation. The various maneuvers of the vehicle that caused the confusion were observed, in particular by T1, who specified: "At times, a light emanated from each..." extremity, red-orange color. From time to time, this bright light seemed to flicker, and this observation was likely due to the different positions taken by this object. Regarding the flickering noted by several witnesses, it is probable that this is an effect caused by the lights of the craft being temporarily behind trees or tree branches during its movements. The key reference point for the witnesses' observations is a small grove; the UFO can appear to be moving relative to this grove and ultimately disappear behind it. We have shown that this is a parallax illusion: the grove is much closer to the witnesses than the UFO, the witnesses' vehicle changes position, so the UFO appears to move relative to the grove, until it disappears behind it. The last point of apparent strangeness is linked to the non-observation of the UFO when T1 and T2 positioned themselves on the CD 116 behind the grove and searched for the UFO. This is primarily explained by the fact that the witnesses logically looked behind the grove on their right and did not think to look to the opposite side, to the left, towards the south. GEIPAN classifies the case as B: probable observation of a forestry vehicle carrying out nighttime maintenance work in a small wood located approximately 2 km south of the witnesses.

summary: Likely observation of flares.
description: On May 10, 1981, witnesses observed a peculiar luminous phenomenon around 8:30 p.m. A red sphere high in the sky appeared to descend gently and land. Suddenly, an intense light burst from a triangle, illuminating the entire area, and then white smoke was seen rising toward the ground. This phenomenon recurred four times in succession, approximately 10 minutes apart. The investigation indicated that the witnesses were likely misled by flares launched on the evening of the second round of the presidential elections.

summary: UFO SIGHTING.
description: On May 5, 1981, around 10:00 AM, a witness reported seeing a black sphere from his home, approximately three kilometers away. This object, three meters in diameter, was moving slowly when it suddenly disappeared. During the investigation, this witness's account proved unreliable, casting serious doubt on the veracity of the sighting.

summary: Observation of flares, probably launched during military maneuvers.
description: On May 4, 1981, between 8 p.m. and 11 p.m., numerous witnesses, including military personnel, observed orange lights in the sky heading towards Switzerland. The investigation established that military maneuvers had indeed taken place that evening near the Swiss border and that the lights in question were flares.

summary: observation of several objects in the sky.
description: On May 4, 1981, several witnesses observed several objects in the sky around 11:00 PM, intermittently emitting intense white lights. The objects were at a great distance and moving from southeast to north. No noise was heard during the observation. One of the witnesses observed the objects through binoculars and was able to make a sketch. No other information has been gathered about this phenomenon, for which we lack details.

summary: Probable observation of atmospheric reentry.
description: On April 26, 1981, around 10 p.m., several witnesses observed a strange luminous phenomenon in the sky. A red, luminous ball accompanied by a few flickering flames moved from east to west. The phenomenon lasted a few seconds before changing shape to resemble a sliver of light and disappearing abruptly. These people likely witnessed an atmospheric reentry.

summary: Probable observation of atmospheric reentry.
description: On April 7, 1981, at approximately 8:00 PM, witnesses observed a fireball at an altitude of about 4,000 meters. This was followed by a colored trail and then appeared to fall in the surrounding area. No other reports were collected. Based on their descriptions of the phenomenon, these individuals likely witnessed an atmospheric reentry.

summary: Multiple observations of the evolution of a multicolored spherical object in the sky of Metz: lack of information.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as A, B, C, or D, which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This case, previously classified as D and named METZ (57) 30.03.1981, is one of a group of cases recently re-examined. It concerns the observation on March 30, 1981, between 11:00 AM and 12:00 PM by six independent witnesses of a UFO flying over certain neighborhoods of the city of Metz (57). Alerted by a newspaper article in the "Republicain Lorrain," the police launched an on-site investigation the day after the incident. The available witness statements strongly suggest a possible case of mistaken identity involving a multicolored party balloon (see the investigation report). Notably, of the six witnesses, four referred to a balloon (a type of balloon) and the other two to a sphere. However, the contradictions and inaccuracies in the testimonies prevent a definitive conclusion from being reached. Furthermore, one might regret the absence of a more thorough investigation, conducted both on-site and by the Gendarmerie, particularly the collection of angular data from witnesses (angular dimensions of the UFO, elevation above the horizon), precise witness positioning, accurate observation durations, a more established chronology, etc. Without this data, nothing allows us to either confirm or refute the hypothesis of a celebratory balloon. GEIPAN classifies the case as Category C, the lack of information preventing a sufficiently in-depth exploration of this otherwise plausible hypothesis.

summary: Observation of a very fast-moving phenomenon
description: On March 28, 1981, between 3:00 and 5:00 PM, two people spotted an object they initially mistook for a fireball. The object was traveling at a very high speed along a northwest-northeast trajectory. Circular in shape, its circumference was approximately 3 to 4 meters. No further information was gathered.

summary: Multiple observations of a probable atmospheric reentry.
description: On February 26, 1981, at approximately 6:30 PM, several witnesses observed a peculiar luminous phenomenon in the sky for a few seconds. A circular, orange shape moved southwest-northeast, followed by a luminous trail. Descriptions and drawings made by these individuals suggest they likely witnessed an atmospheric reentry.

summary: Two fixed luminous spheres
description: On February 23, 1981, a witness leaving his home spotted two large, luminous orbs in the sky. For a few seconds, they emitted a very intense and blinding light. Very surprised by the phenomenon, the witness saw the orbs reappear a few seconds later in the same place before disappearing completely. The witness claims that since this observation, he has experienced health problems (constant fatigue and general malaise). No other accounts have been collected regarding this phenomenon, for which we lack information.

summary: Observation of the Saturn-Jupiter conjunction.
description: Between February 12 and March 11, 1981, several witnesses observed a peculiar light in the sky at night, at the same times each day. This point of light moved very slowly each time, in the same east-southeast direction, and appeared to blink. Verification using astronomy software suggests that the witnesses likely saw the Saturn-Jupiter conjunction, which was particularly visible at the beginning of that year.

summary: probable observation of flares
description: On February 9, 1981, at approximately 2:45 PM, a witness observed an orange fireball in the sky, followed by a trail of gray smoke. This sphere descended slowly and silently, disappearing into the landscape. Another fireball of the same type then appeared. During the investigation, it emerged that on February 9, at approximately 2:30 PM, firefighters from the nearby airport launched distress flares equipped with parachutes. These flares ascend vertically to an altitude of approximately 100 to 200 meters, remain lit for about a minute before gently descending and extinguishing. The witness likely saw these distress flares.

summary: Observation of the silent movement of 3 large pinkish balls in the night sky above the sea: lack of information.
description: The gendarmerie reports an observation made on February 1, 1981, at 2:40 a.m. by a night watchman. During his shift, he spotted three large, dull, pinkish spheres above the sea, forming an isosceles triangle. No flashing lights were seen, and no noise was heard during their movement. No other witness statements were collected. The case was initially classified as unexplained when it was first recorded in 1981. Unexplained cases hold potential for scientific knowledge, provided that their unexplained nature remains valid over time. Therefore, these cases are subject to review. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience acquired in recent years, this review sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. The current review does not allow this case to retain its unexplained status. - We do not have a written and signed statement from the witness who refused to provide one. It has been a fundamental rule at GEIPAN for many years to work from direct and signed testimonies. Any other situation constitutes a failure to ensure the reliability of the testimony. - The testimony is imprecise (no written description from the witness, no questions and answers). Information regarding size, distance, and speed is always subjective and of limited use. It would have been necessary to know the positions in the sky at the beginning and end of the observation and its duration. - Given the limited information, nothing allows us to rule out balloons or children's balloons illuminated by city lights. It was a weekend night, conducive to a festive event. The UFOs are reported as dim and not emitting light, which indeed suggests illumination from the surrounding environment in the middle of the night. The wind was light and coming from the north at 1:00 AM (see the website Infoclimat). A witness who saw the UFOs over the sea (and not directly overhead) primarily perceived a lateral movement from left to right, whether the UFOs were heading due south, carried by the wind from La Valette, or from La Valette towards La Seyne-sur-Mer, as the witness reportedly observed (as recorded in the official report). Furthermore, given the light wind, it may have changed slightly between 1:00 AM and 2:40 AM. The limited evidence does not allow for confirmation of an inexplicable strangeness, especially since the few available details would be consistent with the flight of balloons or children. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies the case as C: lack of reliable information.

summary: Observations of a bright point with color variations and small movements in the night sky: astronomical misinterpretation of Sirius.
description: In addition to processing routine reports, GEIPAN re-examines older cases, originally classified as type D and published on its website. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience acquired over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even an explicit change in classification in an investigation report. This case, formerly known as CLERY SAINT-ANDRE (45) 1981, is one of the cases classified as type D by GEIPAN and was recently re-examined. On January 29, 1981, at approximately 7:15 PM, a witness noticed a very bright point in the sky that he could not explain. The UFO exhibited color variations and small movements. At 7:20 PM, the witness called the gendarmerie to report the event. Two gendarmes immediately went to the main witness's home. Together, they observed the UFO until 9:00 PM. At the end of the observation, the UFO was still visible. A night shift from another brigade later reported that the UFO was still visible at midnight and 4:00 AM. Photographs were taken by the gendarmes, but they turned out to be negative. The descriptions of the observation locations and the UFO are precise, allowing for a more detailed analysis of this case (see the investigation report). It should be noted that the testimonies of the witness and the gendarmes are perfectly consistent, which demonstrates the reality of the phenomenon. The case is consistent (three witnesses, including two gendarmes), and the description of the observed UFO is quite precise, except for its altitude in the sky, which can be described as low by deduction from other indications (e.g., between the horizon and the lowest star). The described phenomenon shares many characteristics (duration of observation, shape, size, color) with a well-known astronomical object: Sirius. Indeed, Sirius was located exactly in the direction of the main observation (from 7 PM to 9 PM). The main witness rejects the hypothesis of mistaking it for a star, because the UFO changes color and moves erratically, but: - Sirius's angular altitude remains low throughout the observation (from 20 minutes to 9 PM), and this can explain the twinkling (effects of light rays passing through the atmosphere) with a color palette entirely consistent with the witnesses' statements. - The other unusual aspect of the movements (limited amplitude) could be due to the twinkling or could result from the autokinetic effect (see the article on the autokinetic effect). The mention of the UFO's presence at midnight and then at 4 AM is consistent with the Sirius hypothesis. Indeed, this was only noted by another gendarmerie team, which is not reported as having made the initial UFO observation. Sirius was then no longer in the southeast direction reported for the UFO. On the other hand, it is very likely that this second team noticed another strange phenomenon in the sky created by Jupiter in conjunction with Saturn. Indeed present in the southeast, Jupiter surpassed the other stars in brightness and presented a double glow that evening due to the conjunction. This second team could legitimately have thought that this strange glow was that of the UFO reported to him in the Southeast at 9 PM. The very high degree of consistency between all the observations and the view that Sirius could have given on the evening of the observation from 7 PM to 9 PM (and that which could have been given by the Jupiter-Saturn conjunction at midnight and 4 AM) leaves little doubt about the confusion with Sirius regarding the main observation between 7 PM and 9 PM. The strangeness produced by Sirius is quite classic (flickering and/or autokinetic) and remains the source of many misinterpretations (see the GEIPAN website with the keyword Sirius, see also, for example, the case of Grand-Couronne (76) 17.04.2016). Consequently, GEIPAN classifies the case in A: observation of Sirius.

summary: Observation of a bright point moving very quickly
description: On January 26, 1981, at approximately 11:15 PM, a CB radio operator in his car spotted a flash of light in the clear, cloudless sky, lasting for three seconds. Intrigued, he leaned out of his car door and saw a bright white point that rapidly grew larger as it descended. The observation lasted six to seven seconds. The emitted light became significant and then abruptly disappeared. The limited information gathered from this description nevertheless suggests the observation of a probable atmospheric reentry.

summary: Observation in the fog of the movement of a luminous ball in the sky: astronomical mistake with the Sun.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. Its publications include older cases, originally classified as type C, which are now being re-examined solely to improve the relevance of the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience acquired over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even an explicit change in classification in an investigation report. This particular observation was classified as type C in 1981 by GEIPAN. On January 24, 1981, at 9:10 a.m., while driving, a witness spotted, despite the fog, a bright yellow sphere. It was moving in a northwest-southeast direction. Located high in the sky, the object appeared to be rotating. This sphere disappears into the landscape. This case is moderately consistent (only one witness), and the description of the observed UFO is precise. The witness's sincerity and credibility have never been questioned. The described phenomenon shares many characteristics (duration of observation, shape, size, color) with a well-known astronomical object: the Sun, seen through fog. Furthermore, the Sun was indeed present in the observed area of the sky, as was the fog. It is not the witness's visual perception that is at issue, but rather the witness's interpretation of their observation based on their feelings (astonishment, driving through the fog). In the current GEIPAN classification, this case of weak strangeness is classified as UFO A, an observation linked to a misidentification of the Sun as seen through fog.

summary: Observation of a round-shaped glow in the eastern sky: astronomical observation of the Moon.
description: This observation case is classified as C by GEPAN and has been re-examined (see the Investigation Notes document). On January 23, 1981, around 9 PM, a witness returning home from work on a moped was intrigued by a large, round shape in the eastern sky. This shape emitted an intense orange light. According to the witness, it changed position and then disappeared abruptly. During the investigation, no other testimonies were collected. This case is somewhat inconsistent (single witness, short observation), but the description of the observed UFO is quite precise. The witness's sincerity and credibility have never been questioned. The described phenomenon shares many characteristics (shape, size, color) with a well-known astronomical object: the Moon at moonrise. Furthermore, the Moon was indeed visible in the observed area of the sky. It is not the witness's visual perception that is at issue, but rather the witness's interpretation of their observation based on their feelings (fatigue, driving at night on frozen ground, presence of fog). In the current GEIPAN classification, this case of a minor anomaly is classified as "A," an observation linked to a misidentification of the Moon.

summary: Observation of a glow coming from a flare stack at a refinery.
description: On January 19, 1981, around 3:00 a.m., witnesses heard a rumbling sound and felt significant vibrations. Some also saw pink glows in the sky above a factory. After investigation, the phenomenon was identified as originating from the commissioning of a new structure at a refinery in the area. It was explained that the glows in the clouds came from a new flare lit that night.

summary: Observation of the joint movement of three bright points in the night sky: observation of satellites.
description: In March 2012, GEIPAN received a questionnaire reporting an observation made on January 15, 1981, at 5:50 a.m. in Perpignan. That morning, just before going to work, a witness was intrigued by the south-to-north passage, in the clear sky, of three luminous points perfectly aligned and equidistant from each other. The observation lasted three minutes before the points disappeared from the witness's field of vision. Only one witness account was collected. This account was given 35 years after the observation. The case presents little unusual features. The time, duration, and trajectory are consistent with satellites. What surprised the witness was the effect of a group of satellites, which could result either from a swarm of closely spaced and collaborating satellites, or from completely separate satellites orbiting in parallel planes. The second hypothesis is the most likely because swarms did not exist in 1981 (except perhaps on classified US programs). This hypothesis assumes, in principle, a greater angular separation between objects than in the case of the swarm, but this is difficult to clarify given the age of the report. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies the case as B: satellites.

summary: Observations of the silent movement of an elongated, "fire-colored" object at dawn: probable observation of contrails from an aircraft flying at high altitude, illuminated by the rising sun.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as A, B, C, or D, which are now being re-examined to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This observation, previously classified as D and named CALAIS (62) 1981, is one of a group of cases recently re-examined. On January 9, 1981, around 9:00 AM, three witnesses working at a retirement home observed an elongated, yellow-red object moving east-west in the sky. This object was moving at very high speed, but no sound was heard. During the observation, which lasted 3 to 4 minutes, the object was hidden by clouds. It should be noted that two of the witnesses observed the same phenomenon the previous day. It is important to know that all the buildings were demolished starting in 2013, making it impossible to determine the exact building in which the witnesses were located (however, two extreme possible positions were considered in the investigation report). The UFO observed by the witnesses has all the characteristics of a condensation trail produced by an aircraft traveling at high altitude and illuminated by the rising sun (see the investigation report): - cigar-shaped or oval, similar to photographic examples of such trails; - fiery or red/orange/yellow color, typical of the color such trails take on when illuminated by the sun low on the horizon (at sunrise or sunset). - movement similar to that of a very distant object, at a great distance, as noted by witness 1. It is relatively common, under similar lighting conditions (sun low on the horizon) and in very stable atmospheric conditions at high altitude, for the condensation trail of an airliner to produce this type of visual effect, of which GEIPAN now possesses numerous photographic testimonies. The common characteristics are that the aircraft producing these short condensation trails were photographed around dawn or dusk, with the sun near the horizon, which produces a yellow-orange color on the trails (which can even sometimes be red) and therefore this impression of fire noted by one of the witnesses. In 1981, GEIPAN did not have the experience, acquired and verified today, of this type of testimony created by aircraft contrails. This led to the case being classified as unexplained at the time. The aircraft itself may or may not be visible, and when it is, it is often in the form of a very bright point preceding the contrails (see examples 7 and 9 of contrails). Most of the time, this bright point appears only fleetingly, depending on the geometry of the surface reflecting sunlight and the aircraft's movement relative to the observers' position. The witnesses did not observe this phenomenon, but the UAP was only visible intermittently, occasionally obscured by clouds. As for these contrails, they can take on a more or less elongated shape, V-shaped, spindle-shaped, or even oval, which corresponds well to the witnesses' descriptions of the UAP's shape (cigar-shaped, circular, oval). When the aircraft in question made a turn, the perspective was undoubtedly more favorable, making the separation between the two contrails more visible. This gave one witness the impression that at that moment, it appeared to be cut in two. Finally, Witness 1 noted the presence of two white trails before the UFO disappeared. This mention of white trails confirms the hypothesis of confusion with the contrails of an aircraft. Thirty-seven years later, it remains impossible to identify the original aircraft. But since the observation was made at low altitude (it is indeed low on the horizon that these ochre trail colors can appear at sunrise or sunset), the aircraft could have been located on a beach 50 to 150 km east of Calais. This encompasses a significant air traffic area in 1981 and leaves a reasonable possibility of finding an aircraft that had followed a trajectory with a more or less pronounced turn. The consistency of the witness testimony is rather weak. There are indeed three witnesses, but their accounts are interdependent, providing few quantifiable details (no angular data, for example). The qualitative information provided is sufficiently characteristic to validate the explanation. In conclusion, GEIPAN classifies the case as B: probable observation of contrails from an aircraft flying at high altitude, illuminated by the rising sun.

summary: Observation of the landing and departure of an object that left traces on the ground.
description: On January 8, 1981, the witness was on the upper terrace of his property, working on the construction of a small masonry building to protect a pump. His attention was suddenly drawn to a whistling sound, and he saw a craft descend towards the ground, land a few dozen meters below him, and then take off again after a few seconds along a vertical trajectory before disappearing at high speed from his sight. Beneath the craft, the witness noticed prominent circular shapes that he identified as hatches or feet. The craft, gray like zinc, emitted neither flame nor smoke and was approximately 2.5 meters long and 1.7 meters high. It was circular, with a thicker band around its diameter, and the "feet" were about the size of a mason's bucket. The entire observation lasted between 30 and 40 seconds. When the witness approached the landing site, he observed a track approximately 2 meters in diameter on the ground with skidding marks at certain points around its circumference. The Gendarmerie intervened on January 9th, interviewed the witness, confirmed the track on the ground, and collected soil samples from the track itself, as well as samples of wild alfalfa plants progressively from the track to a distance of approximately 10 meters. GEPAN intervened on February 17th. The tracks were still visible, and a new series of alfalfa and soil samples was taken. The soil analyses were entrusted to four different laboratories, each using different techniques and providing a complementary perspective. The synthesis of these analyses highlights three main findings: significant soil compaction indicating the presence of a heavy object that left a slight deposit of iron and iron oxide, as well as phosphates and zinc, possibly resulting from the friction of a paint coating on the soil; the very black residues observed on the track, which could be combustion residues; and significant heating (but less than 600°C). Biochemical analyses of the alfalfa samples were carried out by an INRA biochemistry laboratory. These analyses showed multiple forms of plant degradation correlated with their distance from the track. The causes of this degradation were not determined, but the hypothesis of an intense electric field can be considered. The analyses conducted have yielded little in the way of a quantitative estimate of the phenomenon, nor any proof of the witness's account, which remains unique, although the witness's behavior leaves no room for doubt regarding their credibility. A significant and unusual phenomenon occurred that day, and the investigation has not been able to determine its origin.

summary: Observation of a plate-shaped object
description: On January 1, 1981, at approximately 9:40 PM, two police officers spotted a luminous phenomenon that intrigued them. Between 100 and 150 meters in the sky, a yellow-orange glow shimmered. While observing the progression of this light, they saw a circular object rotating on its axis, which, at a steady, slow, and silent speed, appeared to begin a descent. The object emitted several flashing lights and left a short trail behind it. The observation, which lasted about a minute, ended when the object was obscured by the landscape. No further information was gathered about this phenomenon, which remains unexplained.
